title: Becoming Easier to Love
summary: Sometimes growth is not becoming more impressive. It is becoming the kind of person whose presence does not make other people brace themselves.
excerpt: Sometimes growth is not becoming more impressive. It is becoming the kind of person whose presence does not make other people brace themselves.
paragraphs: Sometimes the clearest mirror is not what people say when they are angry. It is what slips out when they are trying to be careful. "I did not know how you would take it." "I almost did not bring it up." "I waited for a better moment." Sentences like that can tell you something about the weather people experience around you.

That is not always easy to face. Most of us prefer to think about love in terms of whether we chose the right people, whether we were understood, whether we were given enough patience. Those questions matter. But there is another one that grows sharper as you get older: what is it like to be close to me when something difficult needs to be said?

A person can be loyal and still exhausting to love. Present and still hard to approach. Good-hearted and still so quick to defend themselves that everyone around them learns to edit the truth before speaking. Sometimes the problem is not a lack of love. It is the atmosphere our pain, pride, hurry, or defensiveness keeps creating.

Many of these habits make sense once you know where they came from. If mistakes were punished, you may have learnt to argue before you are accused. If your needs were often dismissed, you may have learnt to become distant before anybody can disappoint you. If tenderness was inconsistent, you may have learnt to stay guarded, sharp, funny, busy, or right. Old protection can look very reasonable from the inside.

The difficulty is that what protected you in one season can make closeness expensive in another. The people nearest to you should not always have to measure their tone before they tell the truth. They should not have to guess which version of you will answer the door. They should not have to work so hard to keep peace with you that they stop feeling fully known around you.

Becoming easier to love does not mean becoming weak, agreeable, or endlessly available. It does not mean saying yes to poor treatment or pretending nothing hurts. It means your honesty no longer needs cruelty to feel clear. It means your boundaries can stay intact without turning the room cold. It means somebody can bring you a concern without feeling as though they are stepping onto a minefield.

A lot of real growth looks quieter than people expect. It looks like listening without building your defence while the other person is still on their second sentence. It looks like apologising cleanly. It looks like asking one more question before assuming the worst. It looks like noticing that somebody has gone quiet around you and caring enough to wonder why.

There is something deeply kind about becoming safer for other people. Not perfect. Not endlessly calm. Just safer. The sort of presence that makes a child tell the truth sooner, a spouse exhale, a friend risk honesty, a colleague stop bracing for embarrassment. That kind of steadiness changes more than our cleverness ever will.

Maybe that is one of the less glamorous forms of maturity. Not becoming more impressive, but becoming less difficult to receive. Less sharp when tired. Less proud when corrected. Less defended when love is trying to reach you in a form you did not control. Strong enough to stay open.

You do not fix that in one dramatic moment. It is usually smaller than that. One softened reply. One honest apology. One decision not to punish somebody with distance because your feelings were hurt. Growth is not only becoming stronger. Sometimes it is becoming easier to love, and the people closest to you will feel the difference before you know how to name it.
